title: Every module is a directed colimit of finitely presented modules
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-module. There exist a small nonempty directed partially ordered set $I$, finitely presented $R$-modules $M_i$ for $i\in I$, transition maps $f_{ij}:M_i\to M_j$ for $i\le j$, and compatible maps $f_i:M_i\to M$ identifying $M$ with the colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] of this directed system. Here finitely presented means the cokernel of an $R$-linear map between finite free $R$-modules [def-sc-finitely-presented-module].

source.place: Tag 058G, theorem-lazard proof: paragraph beginning 'First recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules'

proof.text: Put $S=M$ as a set, and let $P$ be the $R$-module of finitely supported functions $S\to R$, with pointwise operations and coordinate vectors $e_m$ for $m\in M$. Every $v\in P$ has the unique finite expansion $v=\sum_m v_m e_m$, so these vectors are a basis in [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Define $p:P\to M$ by $p(v)=\sum_m v_m m$. Finite sums show that $p$ is $R$-linear, and $p(e_m)=m$ proves surjectivity. Let $K=\{v\in P:p(v)=0\}$, an $R$-submodule.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 1

proof.text: For a finite subset $J\subset S$, write $P_J\subset P$ for the vectors supported on $J$; restriction of coordinates identifies it with $R^J$. Let $I$ consist of pairs $(J,N)$ with $J\subset S$ finite and $N\subset P_J\cap K$ a submodule that is the span of a finite list of vectors. Order these pairs by $(J,N)\le (J',N')$ if $J\subset J'$ and $N\subset N'$, taking submodules inside the fixed module $P$. This is a partial order: reflexivity and transitivity are inclusion laws, and inclusion in both directions gives equality of both components. It is a set, since its pairs lie in $\mathcal P(S)\times\mathcal P(P)$; in a universe containing $R$ and $M$ it is therefore small.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 2

proof.text: The pair $(\varnothing,0)$ lies in $I$, the zero submodule being generated by the empty list. For $(J,N),(J',N')\in I$, the pair $(J\cup J',N+N')$ is an upper bound: the union is finite, concatenating finite generating lists generates $N+N'$, and its vectors are supported on $J\cup J'$ and belong to $K$. Thus $I$ is nonempty and directed. No finite generation of $K$ or of $P_J\cap K$ is asserted.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 3

proof.text: For $i=(J,N)$ set $M_i=P_J/N$ and let $q_i:P_J\to M_i$ be the quotient map. If $n_1,\ldots,n_a$ generate $N$, the map $A_i:R^a\to P_J$, $(c_l)_l\mapsto\sum_l c_l n_l$, has image exactly $N$. Hence $R^a\xrightarrow{A_i}P_J\xrightarrow{q_i}M_i\to0$ is exact: the quotient map is surjective and its kernel is $N$. Enumerating the finite set $J$ identifies $P_J$ with $R^{|J|}$, so this is a finite presentation in precisely [def-sc-finitely-presented-module]. This includes $a=0$ and $J=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 4

proof.text: For $i=(J,N)\le j=(J',N')$, define $f_{ij}:M_i\to M_j$ by $[v]_N\mapsto[v]_{N'}$, using $P_J\subset P_{J'}$. This is well-defined because changing $v$ by an element of $N$ changes its image by an element of $N'$, and it is linear by the quotient operations. The formulas give $f_{ii}=1$ and $f_{jk}f_{ij}=f_{ik}$. Define $f_i:M_i\to M$ by $f_i([v]_N)=p(v)$, well-defined since $N\subset K$. The same formula gives $f_j f_{ij}=f_i$, so these maps form a cocone.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 5

proof.text: To verify the universal property, let $T$ be any $R$-module with compatible maps $c_i:M_i\to T$. For each $m\in S$ let $s_m=(\{m\},0)\in I$, and put $t_m=c_{s_m}([e_m])$. Define $h:P\to T$ by $h(v)=\sum_m v_m t_m$, a finite sum. This is linear, using the unique coordinate expansions of [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. For $i=(J,N)$ and $m\in J$, the arrow $s_m\le i$ and compatibility give $t_m=c_i([e_m])$. Consequently for all $v\in P_J$, linearity gives $h(v)=\sum_{m\in J}v_m c_i([e_m])=c_i(q_i(v))$. The empty $J$ case is the same equality on the zero vector.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 6

proof.text: For $v\in K$, choose a finite $J$ containing its support. The submodule $Rv$ is generated by $v$ and lies in $P_J\cap K$, so $(J,Rv)\in I$. Step 6 gives $h(v)=c_{(J,Rv)}([v])=0$. Thus $h$ vanishes on $K$. Define $u:M\to T$ by $u(p(v))=h(v)$: surjectivity of $p$ gives a value at every element, and $p(v)=p(w)$ implies $v-w\in K$, so $h(v)=h(w)$ and the value is independent of the preimage. For $x=p(v),y=p(w)$ and $r\in R$, the equalities $p(v+w)=x+y$ and $p(rv)=rx$ give $u(x+y)=h(v+w)=u(x)+u(y)$ and $u(rx)=h(rv)=ru(x)$. Hence $u$ is linear.

source.place: Tag 058G (theorem-lazard), proof paragraph beginning “For the converse, first recall that any module M can be written as the colimit of a directed system of finitely presented modules”; explicit construction and universal-property verification, part 7

proof.text: For $i=(J,N)$ and $v\in P_J$, Steps 6 and 7 give $u f_i([v])=u(p(v))=h(v)=c_i([v])$, so $u f_i=c_i$ because every class has a representative. If another linear map $u':M\to T$ has these composites, then for every $m\in M$ the singleton stage $s_m$ gives $u'(m)=u'f_{s_m}([e_m])=c_{s_m}([e_m])=u(m)$; hence $u'=u$. This proves existence and uniqueness for every cocone, exactly the definition of colimit in [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Thus the $f_i$ identify $M$ as the colimit of the small nonempty directed system of finitely presented modules constructed above. Uniqueness of a colimit up to unique isomorphism identifies any chosen categorical colimit with this cocone.

lean.statement: theorem exists_directed_colimit_finitePresentation (R : Type u) [CommRing R] (M : Type v) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M] : ∃ (I : Type (max u v)) (p : PartialOrder I) (_ : Nonempty I) (_ : IsDirected I p.toLE.le), ∃ (F : @Functor I (@Preorder.smallCategory I p.toPreorder) (ModuleCat.{max u v} R) inferInstance), (∀ i, Module.FinitePresentation R (F.obj i)) ∧ ∃ (c : Cocone F), c.pt = ModuleCat.of R (ULift.{u} M) ∧ Nonempty (IsColimit c)
lean.note: The index, stage modules, and cocone vertex are placed in the common universe max u v; ULift.moduleEquiv identifies the vertex ULift M with M.
